comments.author: capital_guy
comments.textZhHtml: Genuinely a massive moment in human history. I'm nervous about what comes. as a SWE the gravy train is basically over in my view. they figured out how to make a program that does the job. Always thought i was set for life. difficult to grasp how much life will change in the coming years.

comments.author: elgertam
comments.textZhHtml:
I came close to thinking that way a couple years ago, but I've become more optimistic. There is no shortage of problems that can be solved (in fact, wants are infinite), and LLMs may actually enable our profession to reliably deliver them better than 50% completion.

I've also seen non-technical folks in the corporate and government worlds glom onto vibe coding, only to start flailing like they were caught in a rip current when the underlying technical debt is too strong, even with strong and capable models.

For a certain type of engineer who enjoys really arcane technical problems, yeah, the gravy train may be over, or at least will involve a lot more machines than it used to, as Alan Turing predicted about "mechanical work" becoming a "drudge."[0]

And I think Big Tech is for the foreseeable future a sink for capital in the form of specialized hardware rather than human capital.

[0]https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Alan_Turing#Quotes

comments.author: marsten
comments.textZhHtml:
The arcane technical problems aspect of the job has always been changing; LLMs are just a continuation of the trend.

I'm old enough to remember when compiled languages like C were bemoaned by people because their skill at crafting assembly by hand was suddenly less important. Or similarly with people who were brilliant with arithmetic, or symbolic manipulation, or manual drafting/lettering. These skills were all paramount at one time, and it's natural that the people who excelled at them will feel a sense of loss.

The real goal, however, will always be to solve real-world problems. Engineering consists of whatever gets you there most effectively.

comments.author: SomaticPirate
comments.textZhHtml:
Bullish on AI in the long to medium term but that doesn’t change the fact that it’s displacing junior level jobs now.

Several students I have been trying to help enter the field are facing greater barriers than I have ever seen. Not just leetcode but dozens of interviewing rounds. The problems that they are asked also feel increasingly hard and it seems like interviewers are using AI during the interview while forbidding the interviewee from leveraging any external aids.

We are really burning the next class of developers with the current interview process

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
> Not just leetcode but dozens of interviewing rounds.

I cannot believe that companies are still using leetcode. That's just complete idiocy. The game is all about reading and understanding code now. Anyone who is still conducting timed code trivia examinations has completely lost the plot.

Stop cargo-culting your interview process, and use your brains!

comments.author: tgma
comments.textZhHtml:
This is a classic fallacy: that interview should look the same as the job. There is no reason[1] your evaluation pipeline has to necessarily resemble the task you are hiring for. You could test people on random cognitive tasks and predict their job performance.

[1]: Purely technical. There may be social reasons or legal consequences like "disparate impact" theories coming at you.

comments.author: mlyle
comments.textZhHtml:
Sure, random cognitive tasks are correlates of technical job performance.

But there's plenty of people with high intelligence and problem solving that aren't good programmers, so we probably want to try to hone in on that a little bit instead of picking something with positive correlation.

There are also tall people who are not great basketball players, and vice versa. If you can't do anything but measure height, maybe you should pick for your team that way... but if you aren't so restricted there's surely better ways to go.

comments.author: tkamat29
comments.textZhHtml:
Why would you want to hone in on finding "good programmers" though? Programming is not the end-all be-all skill of being a good software engineer, this was true even before AI but is even more true now.

Leetcode is popular because:

1. It gauges problem solving ability and pattern recognition, which are essential to any job, and particularly useful for software engineers.

2. It is language agnostic - most jobs would rather have a strong engineer that doesn't know their particular language/tech stack than a weak engineer that is familiar with the stack.

3. It has objective evaluation criteria (correctness + time/space complexity).

It's certainly not perfect, but I have yet to see an alternative that accomplishes all of the above. The one thing I can see potentially complementing it is the new style of AI-assisted assessment where you are dropped into an unknown codebase, and asked to make fixes/features that are assisted by an AI agent. This solves the language-agnostic issue with pre-AI versions of these interviews, where you had to have memorized specific tech stack features or language syntax in order to accomplish the task. Now AI can take care of that stuff, and the interviewee can focus on the problem solving aspect.

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
> It gauges problem solving ability and pattern recognition, which are essential to any job, and particularly useful for software engineers.

Proof of claim required. Leetcode primarily measure's someone's ability to memorize leetcode problems, and secondarily measures their ability to vomit this knowledge up in a stressful situation.

There's an entire test-prep industry surrounding this interview method. Any undergrad will tell you that the way you pass leetcode interviews is to "grind". You'd have to be oblivious to not realize that the system has been gamed to hell and back.

Since you are just asserting things, I will assert a simpler explanation: the primary reason Leetcode is popular is because it is cheap. If you have the problem that you have too many applicants and don't want to spend money interviewing them all, you have to come up with an efficient filter that doesn't violate hiring laws. You don't particularly care if the false negative rate is high, so a test of superficially relevant trivia is what you do. Even better if the trivia can be validated by computer!

Setting aside the fact that almost no companies actually had this problem outside of FAANG, thanks to AI, the approach has gone from "somewhat relevant" to "completely irrelevant" within a couple of years. It's time to take it out back and shoot it.

comments.author: 01CPMD3174
comments.textZhHtml:
Leetcode is popular because it gives hiring teams an objective 1)getting people to self select out of the process and 2)shortlisting the people who do opt-in.

I’m sure the companies know that Leetcode is not a great indicator for likelihood to succeed in the role. If they had a perfect information about people, then would stop interviewing at all and just take the best people who applied.

They don’t have perfect information. The information is highly asymmetric. The companies are just trying to not be efficient and not get burned.

It sucks for candidates. But it makes sense for companies when they thousands of applicants they know effectively nothing about.

comments.author: filipdobro
comments.textZhHtml: Leetcode interviewing is popular because it barely requires any effort by the interviewer. It is a small, localized knowledge check of your DSA skills. No other profession requires you to invest this much time into the interviewing process. How about we look at past achievements, contributions and certifications, like in any other field?

comments.author: TeMPOraL
comments.textZhHtml:
> How about we look at past achievements, contributions and certifications, like in any other field?

In other fields, those things aren't nearly as meaningless and easy to game as they are in ours.

comments.author: filipdobro
comments.textZhHtml: I don't agree with that. No mechanic shop will test if you actually know how to change the brakes of a car. They have to gauge it from the interview process without doing the actual work.

comments.author: mlyle
comments.textZhHtml: The mechanic shop will figure out you don't know what you're doing really, really quickly though.  Whereas when we hire someone it's often much longer before we get quality feedback.

comments.author: jjav
comments.textZhHtml:
> Leetcode is popular because:

Well, no. It rewards ability (and free time) to repeatedly work through problems and memorize the solutions. And it rewards acting skills so you can perform like you're discovering solutions on the fly, that you've actually memorized.

That's all it does.

comments.author: tgma
comments.textZhHtml:
Weeding out smart non-programmers is quite easy. Obvious by their resume and their non-coding interviews. I bet in an unlikely scenario that you fail to detect that, you probably have a pretty good hire who'll learn in a heartbeat.

What you really want to weed out, at least at top-tier companies who can afford to be more selective, is people who have a resume, but are not that great at fundamentals. Most loud complaints seem to be of this nature: guy had N years of experience at previous company/is author of popular software, but couldn't get through basic linked list/recursion/BFS--as if this is not an acceptable bare minimum expectation of a professional in the field.

Often people are too polite to say it out loud, but realistically, that is exactly when it is working as intended.

comments.author: miroljub
comments.textZhHtml: It's not. In 99,99% of programming jobs you will never have to implement a linked list. And yet, interviewers pretend it's important to be able to write it on the blackboard.

comments.author: tgma
comments.textZhHtml: Not the point. If you have way more applicants than roles and you are paying well, given the choice between a programmer who cannot implement a linked list [really?] and one who can, you would hire the one who has that ability, even if all they do all day is to stare at Claude Code.

comments.author: montag
comments.textZhHtml: Leetcode is and has always been a conveniently disguised IQ test.

comments.author: tptacek
comments.textZhHtml: People love saying this, but it doesn't make any sense. There are software firms that, within the past 15 years, broadly screened all candidates with actual IQ tests. There's no reason to disguise them at all. The reason nobody in the industry does this is that we all know what a debacle it would be to screen primarily on IQ tests rather than "can people do the job effectively".

stories.title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
stories.titleZh: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
stories.author: speedping
summaryZh: Executive SummaryWiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.Responsible disclosure timelineOctober 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.OverviewWiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.What is NGINX?NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.The VulnerabilitiesBoth vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.Tracking IDThe bugWhat an attacker can achieveCVE-2026-123633HTTP/2 connection use-after-freeExecute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.CVE-2026-123007HTTP/2 send_window integer underflowExecute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.ImpactOn affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.Illustrative deployment: an attacker exploits NGINX to run code on the server, putting the applications and data it serves at risk.Coordinated disclosureWe reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.Vulnerabilities Addressed in the ReleaseF5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table): CVEDescriptionImpactCVSSAffected VersionsCVE-2026-123007Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow controlExploitable in default configurations with HTTP/2 enabled9.21.9.5-1.31.8CVE-2026-123633UAF in HTTP/2Exploitable configured with HTTP/2 as a proxy server9.21.19.7-1.31.8CVE-2026-121810UAF in HTTP/3Exploitable configured with HTTP/3 as a proxy server9.21.25.0-1.31.8CVE-2026-123634UAF during response processing in DNS resolverRCE when attacker controls upstream host name9.20.6.18-1.31.8CVE-2026-113425UAF in mail proxy moduleRCE when configured as a mail server proxy with auth_http9.20.5.33-1.31.8CVE-2026-118899Infinite loop while reading client request bodyPotential denial-of-service when server supports TLS 1.38.71.13.0-1.31.8CVE-2026-120993NULL pointer dereferenceDenial-of-service when configured with proxy_protocol v26.91.31.4-1.31.8CVE-2026-125283Buffer overflow when using alias with try_filesTheoretical RCE in uncommon nginx.conf configuration6.90.9.6-1.31.8CVE-2026-123640Insufficient validation in stream ssl_prereadSSRF-like access when configured with ssl_preread6.91.15.2-1.31.8CVE-2026-120967Client certificate bypassClient certificate bypass in specific SNI configurations6.31.25.5-1.31.8Mitigation and detectionIdentify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.ProductCVE and first affected version or branchFixed releasesNGINX OSSCVE-2026-123633: 1.19.71.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainlineNGINX PlusCVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.037.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1NGINX OSSCVE-2026-123007: 1.9.51.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainlineNGINX PlusCVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.037.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives.Test application compatibility, reload NGINX, and confirm the old workers have exited.Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.Technical deep diveCVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusableNGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1);if (h2c->state.incomplete) { return;}When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.Triggering the use-after-freeNext, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection(). When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.From use-after-free to remote code executionThe freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflowReturning credit for unsent dataHTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window.When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:h2c->send_window += window;This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.A bounds check that no longer worksThe next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.From an invalid length to remote code executionThe invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.ExploitationTo confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.How Can Wiz Help? Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. ConclusionWith NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.Stay in touchHi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

stories.title: AI is killing All About Berlin
stories.titleZh: AI is killing All About Berlin
stories.author: grey-area
summaryZh: Posted on May 26, 2026 Psst! There is an update to this post.

This is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews. When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic. What it means to be first on Google It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future. It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities. If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went. This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it. It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads. I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.

Do you feel good supporting these companies by giving them money every month?

What do you think will happen if these companies become profitable? Do you think it will have a positive effect on our society?

Personally I feel that I'm living with severe chronic cognitive dissonance - and have been for many months at this point. But I'm not sure what I can do, I have rent to pay and children to feed.

Do you all just not have this feeling? How do you combat it?

AI could be similar. The costs of the bleeding edge are probably enormous. stories.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
stories.titleZh: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
stories.author: subset
summaryZh: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name SystemTo understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations.As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features.Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to blockRightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach.Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in.The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it.Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs.In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve written previously, DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order.The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet.For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of Cloudflare and Quad9, rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court rejected penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order.Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study found that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down.Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the InternetThe French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country.Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible.More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web.The way forwardIf nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs.We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue innovative collaborations to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet.In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France.We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.

comments.author: gerdesj
comments.textZhHtml:
Quite. The public DNS is absolutely the wrong way to go about this. However there is nothing wrong with fiddling with DNS "internally" - that's a different issue.

It's all about truth and messaging.

DNS tells you where something is, no more and no less. When queried, it points to the map and says: "It's there, off you trot". DNS does not care what is there, it is just a guide.

DNS works over port 53/udp+tcp and could be fiddled with in transit. There is a variety of DNS called DNSSEC which, with care, can be trusted to be accurate (for your given value of accurate).

Messaging: As I said, port 53/udp+tcp could be fiddled with if DNSSEC is not in play. There is also DNS over HTTPS or DoH. Now the messaging channel is encrypted. At this point you have the same confidence in security as you do when looking at https web sites.

Now, you can obviously use DoH DNS from anywhere in the world and it will look like ordinary web traffic. Most browsers are already doing this.

Messing with DNS now in Europe is basically fiddling whilst Rome burns - bloody stupid and couterproductive. Hamstringing a service such as Quad9 is at best ridiculous.

stories.titleZh: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
stories.author: werrett
summaryZh: The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.

After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into something completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?

stories.title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
stories.titleZh: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
stories.author: slashdev
summaryZh: Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic. Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little evidence for any other tactic. Google answers first An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches. Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900 US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's. You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent: Search intentQ4 2025Q3 2026 Informational (looking something up)48.42%70.44% Commercial (comparing options)26.30%51.35% Navigational (looking for a site)17.04%34.03% Transactional (ready to buy)10.82%28.64% Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026, keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51 and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time. The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%. Queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. Over a year, queries of five or more words grew from 29.3% to 34.8% of unique desktop queries and from 29.6% to 31.9% on mobile. Three and four word searches are still the most common. What happens to the clicks The strongest evidence is an experiment. Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen gave US desktop Chrome users an extension that put each of them at random into a group. One group saw Google as usual, and another had AI Overviews hidden. The researchers then watched two weeks of real searches in January and February 2026. On searches that would show an Overview, the group that could see them averaged 0.37 clicks to outside websites per search, against 0.62 for the group that couldn't, which the authors report as a 39.8% reduction. Searches ending with no outbound click went from 54% to 73%. Clicks on ads didn't change, which suggests Google takes care not to cannibalize its own revenue. Across all searches, with and without an Overview, the authors put the loss at roughly 18.5% of the organic clicks a site gets from Google. The authors expect the loss to grow as Overviews appear on more searches. This is a randomized controlled trial, the most reliable kind of study for separating cause from correlation or coincidence. The effect was statistically significant for informational searches. The navigational and transactional samples were too small to settle anything. This is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop only. A separate preregistered experiment by Wang and colleagues, with 1,100 people, also found that removing AI Overviews and AI Mode raised clicks to publishers. Observational data points the same way. Pew found people clicked an ordinary result on 8% of visits to a results page with a summary and on 15% without one, and ended their browsing session on 26% against 16%. Pew's comparison isn't a controlled experiment, because the searches that draw a summary tend to be longer and phrased as questions. Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of people shown a result who click it. Across more than 2,000 websites in DataForSEO's panel, the desktop CTR of the first organic result fell from 17.83% in September 2025 to 7.43% in August 2026, a drop of 58%. Mobile fell from 25.17% to 20.80%, a drop of 17%. Desktop lost nearly half its click-through rate in one month, March 2026, and stayed down. Mobile fell about as far over five months, then recovered most of it. These figures come from Table A2 of the report. Desktop plunged from 15.18% to 7.94% between February and March 2026. AI Overviews can't easily explain that step since the report has them almost flat that month, at 42.79% and then 43.38%. A change in the format or quality of the Overviews might explain part of it, though that is speculation on our part. Mobile, meanwhile, sank to 12.96% and then rebounded to 22.49% by May. The report itself says its data "does not establish" whether AI answers, layout changes, or changes in behavior are the cause. Its sample may also be shifting underneath it, since the unique desktop queries it counts fell by a third over the year, from 1.97 million to 1.32 million. Whatever the cause, a top ranking on desktop now earns less than half the clicks it did a year earlier. DataForSEO also estimates where clicks go on pages with and without an Overview. By its model, the first organic result holds 9 to 16 points less click share on pages with one, though these are different searches on a single day's snapshot: Search intent Position 1, no Overview Position 1, with Overview Overview's cited links Informational37.1%20.7%42.4% Navigational33.4%24.1%44.8% Transactional37.6%21.4%43.0% Commercial33.8%21.1%42.2% The click share for the Overview's cited links looks promising, but it comes from a model. Pew, which logged real browsing, saw people click a link inside a summary on just 1% of visits, against 8% for ordinary results. Eighteen months and a large change in the product separate the two measurements, so it is difficult to say which is closer to the truth. Google disputes that search traffic to websites is declining. In August 2025 its head of Search, Liz Reid, wrote that total organic clicks were "relatively stable year-over-year" and that Google was sending "slightly more quality clicks", meaning clicks where people don't quickly come back. She gave no figures to back that up. Your site can't see whether someone goes back to Google, so you can't check Google's quality-clicks claim yourself, but you can check what your Google clicks are worth. RevScope, our product, shows your revenue per visitor from Google, AI Overviews included, and which landing pages earn the most. Who the answers cite If people read the summary and stop there, it matters which sites the summary cites. The report compares Google's AI Overviews with ChatGPT. Their most-cited lists overlap, but a different kind of site leads each one. RankGoogle AI OverviewsCitationsChatGPTAnswers citing it 1youtube.com51.9Mwikipedia.org4.88M 2reddit.com25.1Mreddit.com3.25M 3facebook.com20.4Mfandom.com670K 4wikipedia.org19.9Mbritannica.com486K 5google.com15.9Mnih.gov476K The report warns that the two platforms' counts aren't comparable, so compare where a site ranks within each list. Reddit and Wikipedia rank near the top of both, and by our count 16 of the 30 domains in each top 30 appear on both lists. The differences are still large. YouTube is first in AI Overviews and nineteenth in ChatGPT. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok make Google's top ten and miss ChatGPT's top 30, while Reuters, The Guardian, AP News, and The Washington Post make ChatGPT's top 30 and miss Google's. ChatGPT also often cites nobody: 27.3% of its answers had no source, against 0.7% for AI Overviews. So, as the report puts it, strength on one platform "doesn't automatically guarantee" the same on another. Reddit also appears in Google's ordinary top ten for 32.15% of the report's tracked results, nearly eight times Quora's 4.11%. Two limits apply to all of this. The first is that the answers come from prompts DataForSEO collected, and the report doesn't explain how they were chosen or whether they match what people really ask. The second is that big platforms do about as well in ordinary results: Pew found Wikipedia, YouTube, and Reddit made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries and 17% of those in standard results. Still, the common belief that AI favors Reddit holds up in this data. GEO looks mostly like SEO Google's position is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary", beyond a page being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Since that is a company describing its own product, we looked at outside data on two questions. The first is which sites get considered, and the second is which page on a site gets picked. Which sites: link profiles correlate with citations A referring domain is another website that links to yours. DataForSEO measured how closely referring domains track AI citations using Spearman's correlation, a score where 0 means no relationship between two rankings and 1 means they match exactly. The score was 0.406 for AI Overviews and 0.377 for ChatGPT. Links marked as coming from user-generated content, such as forum posts, scored lower, at 0.342 and 0.314. These are moderate relationships, and they don't show that links cause citations, since large, well-known sites tend to have more of everything. The samples also contain only domains cited at least once, so they can't tell you what it takes to get cited for the first time. A similar pattern shows up in ordinary rankings: domains ranking first had a median of 111 referring domains against 85 for positions 4 to 10, with heavy overlap between the groups. For AI Overviews, the median cited domain had 282 referring domains on the easiest keywords and 1,571 on the hardest, after the report excluded giant platforms like YouTube and Amazon and any domain with fewer than 50 referring domains. Small sites weren't measured at all. The ranges are also wide, at 518 to 5,765 for the middle half of domains on the hardest keywords, so sites with very different link profiles get cited. Which page: cited pages often don't rank for the query Ranking for a query and being cited for it are drifting apart. Ahrefs found 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for that query in July 2025, and about 38% in March 2026. The two studies differ in sample, parsing, and the Gemini model behind the Overviews, so the size of that fall isn't a clean measurement. One possible mechanism is what Google calls query fan-out: its documentation says these features may issue "multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources". A page could then be cited because it ranks for a related question the reader never typed. Ahrefs offers this only as a possibility, and its earlier study tested the idea and found that the data didn't support it. The most careful test of page-level tactics we found is a study by the SEO software company SISTRIX, published in October 2026. It paired 48,527 pages cited by ChatGPT, AI Mode, or AI Overviews with uncited pages from the same site, which removes the site's overall strength from the comparison. In the table, a factor of 2.7 means pages with the feature were cited 2.7 times as often as pages without it. Page featureFactorWhat SISTRIX says about it Current year in the title2.7A rough stand-in for maintained content, not a title trick; an initial indication Table of contents with jump links1.7Only 14% of pages had one; 2.5 on editorial sites FAQ structured data1.5At 833 URLs it pointed the opposite way, a warning about small GEO studies Visible last-updated date1.31.9 on editorial sites, but 0.7 on shops; only 5% of pages showed one Ten or more external links1.3Linking out to sources Product structured data0.80.5 in AI Overviews, but "not a lever, but no cause for concern either"; it should stay Many features combined2.1Against barely optimized pages An experiment in the paper that gave GEO its name points the same way as SISTRIX's correlations. Aggarwal and colleagues rewrote web pages and measured how much of a generated answer drew on them. On their 10,000-query benchmark, adding quotations raised a page's visibility by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31%, and citing sources by about 27%, while keyword stuffing lowered it by about 8%, all on their main measure, the position-weighted share of the answer's words. Lower-ranked pages gained the most: citing sources lifted a page ranked fifth by 115% and cut the top-ranked page by 30%. They also tried Perplexity, an AI search product, on 200 samples, uploading the source text as files rather than letting it search. The gains on that measure were smaller, at about 21% for quotations and 9% for statistics. The main test used GPT-3.5 reading the top five search results, which is well behind today's products, so the percentages are dated even if the direction still holds. The most debated shortcut has nothing behind it so far. llms.txt is a proposed file that tells AI systems what a site contains. SE Ranking analyzed nearly 300,000 domains and found no correlation with citations. SISTRIX also concluded there is "no measurable effect", though it cautions that domains with the file differ from others in many ways, so this part of its data doesn't have the same-site pairing. Google says "you don't need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup" for its AI features. The data agrees about the files, though SISTRIX's FAQ structured data result suggests some markup may help. AI sends little traffic, but it is growing and may convert well AI assistants sent 0.28% of total traffic across 74,752 websites in March 2026, according to Ahrefs. That was about 3.5 million visitors, against 345 million from Google, or roughly a hundred to one. Ahrefs describes it as small but growing fast. The true figure is somewhat higher because some visits, especially from mobile apps, get counted as direct traffic. The same Ahrefs article reports that on its own site, AI search visitors were 0.5% of visitors and 12.1% of signups. Ahrefs sells SEO software, so its audience may be unusually likely to use AI tools, and one site proves little. Still, on that site an AI visitor was about 24 times as likely to sign up as the average visitor. Some of the value never shows up as traffic. People read an AI answer, form an opinion, and never click. To count what AI visits are worth on your own site, RevScope reports when ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and other assistants send visitors and whether they buy. It also tracks when AI and search engine bots crawl your pages. Google's own reporting has a gap too. It counts traffic from its AI features inside the overall "Web" numbers in Search Console. Since 2026 Search Console also has generative AI reports, which Google says show how often your URLs appeared in those features, along with pages, countries, and devices. The announcement describes impressions and doesn't mention clicks, so you learn how often you appear, not how many visits or sales that brings. Rank tracking can't fill the gap, since a page can hold position 1 and earn fewer clicks than it used to. What to do about it Keep the fundamentals. Pages must be indexable and eligible for a snippet. Referring domains correlated with citations more strongly than user-generated links did, and higher-ranking domains had moderately more of them, so links from other sites remain a reasonable investment, even though neither relationship proves cause. Find out who gets cited on your topics, per platform. Check your important queries in AI Overviews and ChatGPT and note the sources. Being described accurately there may matter as much as your own page. Take part in the communities those answers cite, such as Reddit, so that you are mentioned there. Write pages worth quoting. Answer related questions directly, add original data and named sources, and use clear headings. If you run an editorial site, show when the page was last updated. Skip the shortcuts. An llms.txt does no harm but has shown no benefit, AI-specific markup isn't needed, and keyword stuffing lowered visibility in the GEO paper's test. Judge the work by revenue. With fewer clicks to go around, it matters more which ones pay. Tie each channel to the sales it produces rather than to its rank or its visit count. The numbers above are mainly US English, and the products change quickly, so the 2025 figures may already be out of date. Nearly all the large datasets come from companies that sell SEO data or software, including DataForSEO, Ahrefs, SISTRIX, and SE Ranking, and we sell analytics. Almost everything about what earns a citation is correlation. Three findings hold up. Controlled experiments show fewer clicks to outside websites when Google's AI features are present, domains with more referring domains tend to be cited more often among those already cited, and we found no proven shortcut to being cited. Sources Search Insider: 2026 Edition DataForSEO · Annual research report · October 2026 DataForSEO collects search and AI answer data for a living and publishes its tables and methods, which allowed us to check the monthly figures behind its headlines. It sells this data, its answer prompts aren't explained, and its click shares are modeled. We rely on it for what appears where, and treat its click estimates and correlations as indications. Our charts are redrawn from its published values. The Impact of Google AI Overviews on Publisher Traffic and User Experience: Evidence from a Field Experiment Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen · Working paper · SSRN · draft of June 2026 University researchers ran a preregistered randomized experiment on 1,065 US participants, 770 of them in the two groups compared here. Random assignment makes it the best evidence that Overviews themselves reduce clicks. It isn't yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop Chrome for two weeks. We read a copy of the June draft hosted outside SSRN. AI in Search Reduces Publisher Referrals Without Improving User Experience: Experimental Evidence Stephanie T. Wang, Jeffrey Gleason, and colleagues · Preprint · arXiv · August 2026 A second preregistered experiment, with 1,100 people, which independently supports the direction of the result. We read its abstract only, so we use it for that direction and not for any figure. Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results Athena Chapekis and Anna Lieb · Short read · Pew Research Center · July 2025 A nonprofit research organization with no search product to sell, logging the real browsing of 900 consenting US adults. It covers one month, March 2025, re-collected the summaries in April, and doesn't control for which searches draw a summary. AI Features and Your Website and the Search Console reports announcement Google Search Central · Documentation, last updated December 2025, and blog post, June 2026 The primary sources for what Google says its AI features require and how it reports them. They are reliable on those rules, and they aren't independent evidence of what works. AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks Liz Reid · Company blog · Google · August 2025 Google's public position on total clicks, from the person running Search. Google can see the true numbers, but this post publishes none of them, so we report it as a claim. Citation Worthiness: Which GEO Tactics Hold Up Across 96,418 URLs Johannes Beus, Julia Weissbach, and the SISTRIX Content Team · Industry study · SISTRIX · October 2026 Its same-site pairing and correction for multiple testing make it more careful than most GEO studies. It sells SEO software, covers only German-speaking markets, and reports correlations. GEO: Generative Engine Optimization Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, and colleagues · Conference paper · KDD 2024 · version 3, June 2024 The academic paper that named the field and ran controlled rewrites of pages. It shows content changes can move visibility, but its test engine is now dated, and its authors' "up to 40%" should not be read as a current forecast. Update: 38% of AI Overview Citations Pull From The Top 10 and 76% of AI Overview Citations Pull From the Top 10 Louise Linehan with Xibeijia Guan · Industry studies · Ahrefs · March 2026 and July 2025 Ahrefs sells SEO tools and tracks AI answers through its Brand Radar product, here matching about 4 million cited URLs against rankings in the later study. The two studies aren't like-for-like. The 38% counts results in every part of the page; for ordinary links alone it is 37.1%. AI Chatbot Traffic: What It Is, and How to Get More Mateusz Makosiewicz · Company blog · Ahrefs · May 2026 The source for the 0.28% figure, from analytics on 74,752 sites, and for the signup figure from Ahrefs' own site. It gives conflicting percentages for Google's share in different places, so we compare visitor counts instead. LLMs.txt: Why Brands Rely On It and Why It Doesn't Work Yulia Deda · Industry study · SE Ranking · page dated October 2026 A large correlation study of nearly 300,000 domains. It doesn't name the AI platforms it sampled, so we use it only alongside SISTRIX and Google's statement.
